title: Speaking Truth Without Creating Enemies
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer treats truth-telling as one of the most delicate leadership skills, drawing on her own experience of being sidelined for naming root issues when those in authority lacked answers. Her lesson is that insight carries responsibility and delivery matters: truth offered without care provokes defensiveness, while truth offered with clarity, steadiness and respect invites responsibility. She frames the key distinction as being right versus being effective, and warns that the victim-bully-rescuer dynamic entrenches positions and creates enemies where partners are needed. Grounded truth, in her account, names reality while staying in relationship and leaves others room to step into responsibility. She applies this to the Los Angeles fires and systemic failure more broadly, and closes with reflection questions on holding back truth.
points: Schafer's central distinction is between being right and being effective, which she names as where many leaders get stuck.
Truth delivered without care provokes defensiveness, whereas truth delivered with clarity, steadiness and respect invites the listener to take responsibility.
Casting truth-telling as victim, bully and rescuer produces blame and quick fixes that entrench positions rather than create lasting change.
Grounded truth names reality without assigning villains or claiming moral superiority, keeping the relationship intact.
quotes: What I learned, often the hard way, is that truth is not always welcome, particularly when those in positions of authority do not yet have the answers, or are unwilling or unable to develop them. In those moments, truth can feel threatening rather than helpful.

As I studied different modalities and leadership frameworks, I came to understand something essential: insight carries responsibility, and delivery matters. Truth that is offered without care can provoke defensiveness. Truth that is offered with clarity, steadiness, and respect invites responsibility.

Someone is harmed, someone is blamed, and someone rushes in to fix. While this pattern may feel satisfying in the short term, it rarely produces lasting change. More often, it entrenches positions and creates enemies where partners are needed.
It does not assign villains or seek moral superiority. It names reality while remaining in relationship. It creates space for others to step into responsibility rather than pushing them into defense.
It is easy to ignore issues until they happen to you. That pattern must end, because these systemic failures are happening to all of us.

For those currently enduring profound loss, and for those of us who are one dry, windy night away from the same fate, this is that moment. Speaking truth now is not about blame or alarm, it is about refusing to repeat the same patterns while expecting a different result.
